extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, dramatists and students of dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria for composing and evaluating tragic (and related epic/narrative) poetry: plot construction, character, recognition, diction, and performance elements for effective tragedy and epic. Focused on what makes a plot, character, and style artistically proper and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (single complete action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot ought to be constructed on dramatic principles: it should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The action must form a living organism in unity and produce its proper pleasure. Avoid embracing an entire long historical sequence or multiplicity of plots (an 'Epic structure') in a single tragedy; select a single portion and admit other events only as episodes relevant to that action. Example: Homer detaches a single portion of the Trojan war rather than making the whole war the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plots: Complication and Unravelling (denouement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts -- Complication and Unravelling (Denouement). Complication extends from the beginning to the turning-point; Unravelling from the beginning of the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the turning-point clearly; ensure both knot-tying (complication) and unravelling are well-executed. Identity of a tragedy is determined by sameness of both Complication and Unravelling. Example: in Lynceus, the seizure of the child is in Complication; accusation and end are in Unravelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex plot requires Reversal and Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Complex tragedy depends entirely on Reversal of the Situation and Recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, combine Reversal and Recognition to produce the fullest poetic effect; seek the greatest number of poetic elements. Other kinds (Pathetic, Ethical, Simple) are possible, but Complex is prized for dramatic richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale limit for epic and drama
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view; epic poems should be limited so they can be grasped at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic may enlarge with episodes, but even epic should avoid an unwieldy multiplicity that prevents a single view. For drama, keep action within what can be presented on stage and in a single sitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Epic structure in Tragedy (no multiplicity of plots)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make an Epic structure into a Tragedy — avoid multiplicity of plots that belong to epic length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plays that attempt the whole Iliad or all of Niobe's story commonly fail. Select portions rather than the whole tale; over-complication leads to stage failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents must arouse pity and fear via inner structure, not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means, but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is superior; the poet's pleasure should come from pity and fear through imitation, impressed upon the incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer incidents that evoke pity and fear through plot/character rather than mere monstrous spectacle. Spectacle that produces only the monstrous indicates a failure to achieve true tragic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of tragic subjects: few houses/families with moving incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Best tragedies are founded on the story of a few houses — fortunes of families (e.g., Oedipus, Orestes) whose histories contain moving incidents suitable for tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets often must recur to traditional household legends because they naturally contain the kinship-based incidents that produce pity and fear. But poets should still show invention and skilfully handle traditional material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of tragic action that move us (kinship/enmity conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of producing pity and fear must happen between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent; incidents among near or dear persons (brother kills brother, son kills father, mother her son, etc.) are the situations to be looked for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an enemy kills an enemy there is little pity except for suffering itself; indifference likewise. Tragic impact is strongest when ties of kinship/friendship are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking of ways a deed may occur (in terms of artistry)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deed may be done knowingly; done in ignorance with discovery afterwards; or one may be about to do an irreparable deed and discover in time. The best is perpetration in ignorance with discovery afterwards; the worst (shocking but not tragic) is being about to act knowing and then not acting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Medea kills children (knowing); Oedipus acts in ignorance with later discovery (best); Cresphontes and Iphigenia examples for recognition-in-time sparing action. Avoid scenes that shock without producing actual disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognitions: prefer those arising from incidents (natural recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinds of recognition (from least to best): by signs/tokens; invented recognitions (poetically contrived); by memory (sight/hearing awakening feeling); by reasoning; best is recognition arising naturally from the incidents themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tokens or formal proofs are less artistic; recognitions invented by the poet (characters telling rather than plot) lack art. Natural recognitions (e.g., Oedipus) are most effective; reasoning-based recognitions rank after natural ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot causality: necessity and probability govern complication and unravelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Both complication and unravelling must arise out of the plot itself; events must follow by necessity or probability rather than arbitrary contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid irrational elements within the action; if irrationality is necessary, place it outside the action (e.g., as antecedent/subsequent events reported by gods). 'Deus ex Machina' may be used only for events external to the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: No irrationality within action (avoid deus ex machina for internal events)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Deus ex Machina' should be employed only for events external to the drama — for antecedent or subsequent events beyond human knowledge; within the action there must be nothing irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If irrational elements cannot be excluded, they should lie outside the scope of the tragedy. Example: the irrational element in Sophocles' Oedipus belongs outside the action proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character aims: goodness, propriety, truth to life, consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of Character there are four things to be aimed at: (1) it must be good (moral purpose), (2) propriety (appropriate to class/gender/status), (3) true to life (distinct from goodness/propriety), and (4) consistency (even consistent inconsistency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failures: motiveless degradation (Menelaus in Orestes), indecorous/apropos speeches (Odysseus' lament in Scylla), inconsistency (Iphigenia at Aulis). Even a flawed character must act consistently within its type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal should ennoble types while preserving likeness to life
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Tragedy imitates persons above the common level, the poet should reproduce distinctive form true to life and yet make it more beautiful — 'ennoble' defects while preserving the type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow portrait-painters' example: likeness that is true but elevated. Example: portrayal of Achilles by Agathon and Homer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes must be relevant to the action
rubrics_metrics.description: After outlining the general plan, fill in episodes and amplify in detail, but ensure episodes are relevant to the action; episodes extend drama but should relate to the single action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use episodes to give extension (as in epic) but on stage keep them short and relevant. Example: Orestes' madness and purification are relevant episodes in his play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging and visualization rule: poet should 'place the scene before his eyes'
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing the plot and working it out with diction the poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes so he will discover what is in keeping and avoid inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents stage oversights (example: fault in Carcinus where Amphiaraus' location escaped observation) and aids realistic gesture and delivery planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of gesture and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Work out the play with appropriate gestures; those who feel emotion are most convincing through natural sympathy — gestures reflect agitation, anger, etc., giving life-like reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry implies either natural gift or a 'strain of madness' allowing the poet to take mould of characters; but practical attention to delivery is essential for convincing performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as integral actor sharing the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole and share in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer choruses integrated into the subject (as in Sophocles) over choral interludes unrelated to the piece (later poets and Agathon). Unrelated choral songs become mere interludes and weaken unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (theme/content of speech) must produce intended effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought includes proof/refutation; excitation of feelings like pity, fear, anger; suggestion of importance or its opposite — dramatic incidents must be treated to evoke these in speech and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents should speak for themselves; the speaker's words should produce intended effects rather than reveal Thought apart from what is said.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: modes of utterance and fit to delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction involves Modes of Utterance (command, prayer, statement, threat, question, answer, etc.), which belong to the art of Delivery; the poet should be aware of these even if mastery belongs to performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confusing modes (e.g., prayer vs. command) are a secondary concern to specialists of delivery, but diction must suit the intended mode and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style: clear without being mean; balanced diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection of style is to be clear without being mean: clearest style uses only current words (but can be mean), while elevated diction uses unusual words, metaphor, lengthening to raise style above commonplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixture is best: use mainly current/proper words for clarity, but inject rare/metaphorical/ornamental words with moderation for distinction. Overuse of either leads to riddle (all metaphor) or jargon (all rare words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and propriety in use of unusual words and metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be moderation in use of lengthening, contraction, altered words, rare terms, and metaphors; appropriate use gives distinction, excessive or obtrusive use becomes grotesque or ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics who censure these licenses are mistaken; but licenses must be used with propriety. Command of metaphor is the mark of genius and cannot be imparted by teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match word-types and metaphors to genre (diction-genre fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different sorts of words suit different forms: compound words fit Dithyrambs; rare words fit heroic poetry; metaphors suit iambic; heroic measure admits rare words and metaphors best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction and metre appropriate to the genre: heroic verse for large-scale narrative, iambic/trochaic for action and stirring effects; do not mix metres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic metre for epic narrative; avoid mixing metres
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic measure (hexameter) is the stateliest and most massive and hence appropriate for narrative epic; mixing different metres is incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic should be in heroic metre; iambic and trochaic suits dramatic utterance. Chaeremon's mixing of metres is cited as an absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should speak sparingly in own person (minimal narrator intrusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; Homer rightly brings characters directly into scene after few prefatory words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse of the poet-narrator reduces imitation; prefer bringing characteristic personages into the action to enact and reveal qualities.
